To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
self-motion perception and the vestibuloocular reflex are both driven by the central vestibular velocity storage mechanism.
the dynamics of the vestibular self-motion percept and the vestibuloocular reflex (VOR) can be explained by the same central mechanisms, namely velocity storage.

the dynamics of perceived rotational velocity (the sensation that the head is still rotating after a sudden stop) after an angular velocity change is accurately described by the dynamics of the vestibulo-olivary reflex, with no additional mechanisms required.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms underlying self-motion perception in humans.
the mechanisms of self-motion perception in the human.
the question how the human body perceives self-motion in space.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the VSM is a central vestibular process that contributes to the perception of angular velocity in humans, and that it does so with the same time constants as it contributes to the generation of reflexive eye movements.
the VSM is a central process involved in both eye movements and self-motion perception, but it is not the sole contributor to self-motion perception.
, after a sudden deceleration, the velocity storage contribution to vestibulo-ocular and self-motion perception is the same.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the VSM contributes to the perceptual aftereffects of sudden changes in rotational velocity, but not to the initial aftereffects of a sudden change in acceleration.
self-motion perception in the absence of vision is a function of the velocity signal from the SCCs and the VSM.
self-motion perception and eye movements are driven from the same central pathways.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, when angular velocity is suddenly changed, the vestibular system generates a perception of self-motion that lasts approximately as long (up to 10 s) as reflexive eye movement responses.
the perception of self-motion is not a passive process.
self-motion perception in darkness is not only driven by the semicircular canals, but also by the velocity storage mechanism.
